title: Lesson 3: Discovery and Scoping: Listening Before Proposing
description: The craft of discovery: who to talk to, what to watch, which questions surface the real problem, and how to write a problem statement the client agrees with before you propose any solution.

questions.question: Where does the most reliable picture of the real problem come from?
options: The executive who signs the contract and owns the budget
The compliance officer who sets the rules
The consultant's own experience with similar clients
The people who perform the task, watched doing the work
questions.explanation: The people who do the task day to day know where it actually breaks, and they speak more frankly than the sponsor who is selling the project.

questions.question: What is the test of a good problem statement?
options: It is one sentence the client reads and agrees with
It lists each task the agent will perform for the team
It names the model and provider that will be used
It includes the total price and the delivery date
questions.explanation: A good problem statement is one sentence the client reads and agrees with; if the client hesitates, discovery is not finished.

questions.question: Why gather real numbers during discovery?
options: To confirm what the sponsor already estimated from memory
To size and price the work from real counts
To prove the existing process is already efficient
To avoid having to talk to the operators at all
questions.explanation: Sizing from real counts rather than memory is what turns a price into an honest estimate instead of a guess.
